newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MINING UNION READY TO NEGOTIATE IN HUNTER
The miners' union is ready to begin negotiations for enterprise bargaining at the Hunter Valley Number One mine with mine owner Rio Tinto immediately.
A march of mine workers will this morning take a petition of 412 striking CFMEU members from the union's headquarters to Rio Tinto's offices in Sydney.

The petition informs Rio Tinto that all signatories want the union to represent it in enterprise bargaining negotiations. CFMEU president John Maitland said he is ready to negotiate on Rio Tinto's individual contracts.
LABOR DECIDES LANDMINES SHOULD GO
The Federal Opposition has reversed its policy on landmines, urging the government to support the destruction of Australia's landmine stockpile.

Shadow Foreign Minister Laurie Brereton said he will introduce a private member's bill in Parliament, which would require a total ban on the manufacture, stockpile, use and transfer of landmines, except for a bare minimum needed for mine-clearance training.
Mr Brereton has acknowledged at a function in Sydney, that the previous Labor Government could have handled its landmines policy better.
He said Labor lost sight of the most important dimension of its foreign policy - the human dimension - and accepted his share of the blame.
Mr Brereton said Parliament must now debate Australia's role in addressing the global landmines crisis, and he has urged the government to sign the independent Ottawa Convention banning their use.
SMOKERS TOLD: YOU'RE GIVING YOURSELF CANCER
Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge has launched the latest in a series of highly confronting anti-smoking advertisements.
Dr Wooldridge said he expects the ads, which present conclusive evidence of a direct causal link between smoking and cancer, will disturb and shock smokers.
The ad is based on evidence from a Californian research institute, which late last year proved cigarette smoke damages the P53 gene, leading to the development of tumors.
The ad shows cigarette smoke travelling through an artery, and a tumor growing inside a lung.
Dr Wooldridge said the ad buries the myth that there is no direct link between smoking and cancer, a view pushed by cigarette company board members like former New South Wales Premier, Nick Greiner.

"It means next time you see the chairman of WD & HO Wills, the former Premier...Nick Greiner getting up at the annual meeting and saying: 'Look, it's only a statistical link. We don't know that it causes lung cancer,' I hope every journalist exposes that lie," Dr Wooldridge said.
The campaign will be seen on television from tonight.
ALP READY TO NOMINATE COLSTON SUCCESSOR
It is now glaringly obvious that Senator Mal Colston should resign from the Senate, according to the Labor Party's Queensland Secretary Mike Kaiser.
The Labor-turned-Independent Senator is facing fraud charges over the alleged misuse of his official travel entitlements.
Mr Kaiser said in the unlikely event that Senator Colston does stand aside, the ALP would have no trouble filling the vacancy.
"Senator Colston is obviously a person with a very thick hide. We've thought for some time now that he should step aside," he said.
"The Labor Party can pre-select the Senate nominee very quickly, it doesn't take much time under the party's processes and if we're required to do that we can do that quickly.

" Queensland Labor Leader Peter Beattie would then nominate that person in the state parliament and despite what Queensland Premier Mr Borbidge has previously said, we'd expect the Nationals and Liberals to support our nominee."
Mr Kaiser said the ALP probably will not have to consider a replacement for some time.
There is speculation that Senator Colston may resign from the Senate, to ensure his superannuation entitlements are not damaged by any court case against him.
Under current arrangements, Senator Colston would lose his superannuation payments if he is convicted of a crime, and sentenced to more than a year in prison, while still serving as a Senator.
CARNELL EXPRESSES CONFIDENCE IN INQUIRY HEAD

Questions have been raised about the independence of the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) Government-ordered inquiry into the weekend's building demolition disaster at the old Royal Canberra Hospital.
Katie Bender, aged 12, died after being hit by debris from the implosion.
A number of other people who had gathered on the shores of Lake Burley Griffin to watch the demolition were also hit, and injured by debris.
The inquiry will be led by former Commonwealth bureaucract Noel Tanzer.
ACT Opposition Leader Andrew Whitecross said Mr Tanzer has been paid as an adviser to the head bureaucrat in the Chief Minister's Department.
Mr Whitecross has called for Mr Tanzer to be replaced, on the grounds that his payment as an adviser to the Chief Minister's Department raises questions about the independence of the inquiry.
But Chief Minister Kate Carnell said Mr Tanzer has signed a document indicating he has no conflict of interest in taking up the inquirer's role.
WHITLAM HAS NOT FORGIVEN BARWICK
The ire felt by former Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam for his High Court foe Sir Garfield Barwick has not lessened any with the death on the weekend of the former Chief Justice.
It was on Sir Garfield's advice that then Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed the Whitlam government in 1975.
Sir Garfield Barwick was cremated in Sydney yesterday.
Launching his new book "Abiding Interests" in Sydney last night, Mr Whitlam found it hard to say anything he admired about Sir Garfield, and maintained the advice he gave Sir John was invalid.

"It was one of those cases they talk about judical activism - he was creating law. There was no precedent for it and all the reasons he gave didn't apply in that case and nobody respects them now," Mr Whitlam said.
